Fix \((G,T,e)\in\mathcal G_{n,k}\) and suppose \(d_e(G)<\infty\).  By the definition of \(d_e\), \(\lambda_e\) is algebraic over \(K_G\).  Multiplying the covariance identity by \((I_n-\Lambda)^{\mathsf T}\) on the left and by \(I_n-\Lambda\) on the right gives
\[
 \Omega=(I_n-\Lambda)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(I_n-\Lambda).
\]
Thus every disturbance coordinate belongs to \(K_G(\lambda_D)\).  Conversely, all directed coordinates belong to the source field \(L\), and \(K_G\subseteq L\).  Hence
\[
 L=K_G(\lambda_D).
\tag{1}
\]

Choose \(U\subseteq\lambda_D\setminus\{\lambda_e\}\) maximal algebraically independent over \(K_G\), put \(F=K_G(U)\), and enumerate the remaining directed coordinates as
\[
 y=(y_1,\ldots,y_q)=\lambda_D\setminus U.
\]
Because \(\lambda_e\) is algebraic over \(K_G\), it cannot be adjoined to \(U\); maximality therefore implies that every \(y_a\) is algebraic over \(F\).  Equation (1) makes \(L/F\) finite.  It is separable because the characteristic is zero.  If \(p(t)\in K_G[t]\) is the minimal polynomial of \(\lambda_e\), then \(p\) remains irreducible over the purely transcendental extension \(F/K_G\): clearing denominators in a putative factorization over \(K_G(U)\) and specializing \(U\) away from the finitely many denominators would contradict irreducibility over \(K_G\).  Therefore
\[
 [F(\lambda_e):F]=[K_G(\lambda_e):K_G]=d_e(G).
\tag{2}
\]

By \(\mathrm{thm:incidence\mbox{-}localization}\) and \(\mathrm{def:generic\mbox{-}fiber}\), after first localizing at \(S_G\) and then inverting the nonzero elements of \(K_G[U]\), the evaluation map
\[
 F[y_1,\ldots,y_q]\longrightarrow L
\]
has kernel generated by the missing-bidirected residuals.  Let \(g_a\in F[t]\) be the minimal polynomial of \(y_a\).  Write the kernel identity
\[
 g_a(y_a)=\sum_{i\leftrightarrow j\notin B}c_{a,ij}(y)F_{ij}(y),
 \qquad c_{a,ij}\in F[y].
\]
Differentiating and evaluating in \(L\) eliminates the terms multiplied by the vanishing residuals and gives
\[
 g_a'(y_a)\,dy_a
 =\sum_{i\leftrightarrow j\notin B}c_{a,ij}(y)\,dF_{ij}.
\]
Separability gives \(g_a'(y_a)\ne0\).  Hence the evaluated residual gradients span every coordinate covector \(dy_a\), and the residual Jacobian with respect to \(y\) has rank \(q\).  Select residuals \(f_1,\ldots,f_q\) whose \(q\)-by-\(q\) Jacobian determinant \(\Delta\) is nonzero in \(L\).

There are exactly \(d_e(G)\) distinct \(F\)-embeddings of \(F(\lambda_e)\) into an algebraic closure \(\overline F\).  Each extends to an \(F\)-embedding of the finite separable extension \(L/F\): adjoin the remaining algebraic generators successively and choose a root of the transported minimal polynomial at each step.  Every extended embedding satisfies \(f_1=\cdots=f_q=0\) and sends \(\Delta\) to a nonzero element.  It therefore gives a nonsingular isolated zero of the selected square system.  Embeddings that differ on \(F(\lambda_e)\) give distinct \(\lambda_e\)-coordinates.

Partition \(y\) into nonempty blocks indexed by child vertices, and let \(r_v\) be the size of block \(v\).  Then
\[
 1\le r_v\le\operatorname{indeg}_D(v).
\tag{3}
\]
The displayed definition of \(F_{ij}\) shows that a residual is affine-linear in a single remaining block when only one of its two child blocks meets \(y\), and otherwise has degree at most one in each of two distinct blocks.  Decompose the selected square system into connected components of its equation-block incidence graph.  A nonzero monomial in \(\Delta\) matches equation rows to variable columns within each component, so every component has equally many equations and variables.

Consider the component containing \(\lambda_e\).  Let it have \(b\) blocks, \(u\) unary equations, and \(m_H\) binary equations.  Thus its number of variables is
\[
 q_C=u+m_H.
\tag{4}
\]
If \(b>1\), the binary equations form a connected simple graph \(H\) on these blocks.  It is simple because a binary residual is indexed by one unordered pair of child vertices and the symmetric duplicate cannot occur twice among distinct residual rows.  If \(b=1\), there are no binary equations.

The multihomogeneous bound \(\mathrm{lem:multihomogeneous\mbox{-}bezout\mbox{-}isolated\mbox{-}bound}\) bounds the isolated zeros of this component by the coefficient of \(\prod_vX_v^{r_v}\) in
\[
 \left(\prod_{\ell=1}^{u}X_{v(\ell)}\right)
 \left(\prod_{\{v,w\}\in E(H)}(X_v+X_w)\right).
\tag{5}
\]
After subtracting the unary exponents, (5) counts orientations of \(H\) with a prescribed indegree vector.  Fix a spanning tree of \(H\).  Once its
\[
 g=m_H-b+1
\]
non-tree edges are oriented, at most one orientation of the tree realizes the remaining indegrees: the required indegree at a leaf forces its sole remaining tree edge, and deleting that leaf proves the assertion inductively.  Thus (5) is at most \(2^g\).  For \(b=1\), the coefficient equals one and we set \(g=0\).  Every conjugate of \(\lambda_e\) supplies a distinct isolated zero in this query component, while other components cannot create additional queried values.  Hence
\[
 d_e(G)\le2^g.
\tag{6}
\]

A finite acyclic directed graph has a source, since otherwise indefinitely following incoming arrows would produce a directed cycle.  A source has no nonempty child block, so \(b\le n-1\).  The graph \(H\) is simple.  Applying \(\mathrm{lem:tournament\mbox{-}score\mbox{-}fiber\mbox{-}ceiling}\), including its fixed-edge completion by isolated dummy blocks when \(b<n-1\), gives the independent bound
\[
 d_e(G)\le\tau_{n-1}.
\tag{7}
\]

It remains to control \(g\) by the excess budget.  If \(b>1\), equations (3)--(4) imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
 g
 &=q_C-u-b+1\\
 &\le q_C-b+1\\
 &\le\sum_{v\in C}\bigl(\operatorname{indeg}_D(v)-1\bigr)+1\\
 &\le\sum_{v\ne\mathrm{root}(T)}
       \bigl(\operatorname{indeg}_D(v)-1\bigr)+1\\
 &=|D|-n+2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]
The penultimate inequality uses \(\mathrm{ass:arborescence}\), through \(\mathrm{def:graph\mbox{-}class}\): every nonroot vertex has its incoming tree arrow, so every omitted summand is nonnegative, and acyclicity forbids an arrow into the root because the tree already has a directed path from that root to every vertex.  If \(b=1\), then \(g=0\le |D|-n+2\), since \(|T|=n-1\) and \(T\subseteq D\).  Combining (6)--(8) yields
\[
 d_e(G)\le\min\!\left\{2^{|D|-n+2},\tau_{n-1}\right\}.
\]
Finally, \(|D|=|T|+|D\setminus T|\), so \(\mathrm{ass:excess\mbox{-}budget}\) gives
\[
 |D|-n+2=|D\setminus T|+1\le k+1.
\]
This proves both displayed bounds for \(d_e(G)\).  Maximizing over the finite-degree members in the definition of \(D_k(n)\) proves the asserted frontier bound.  At \(n=6\), the established value \(\tau_5=24\) in \(\mathrm{lem:tournament\mbox{-}score\mbox{-}fiber\mbox{-}ceiling}\) gives
\[
 D_k(6)\le\min\{2^{k+1},24\}.
\]
The transcendence-basis reduction and the count in only the query component show explicitly that no zero-dimensionality assumption on the full generic fiber was used.

Put \(d=k+1\) and \(N=2d+2=2k+4\).  In the \(N\)-vertex member of \(\mathrm{def:attaining\mbox{-}family}\), the directed arrows are
\[
 0\to P_i,\qquad 0\to Q_i,\qquad P_i\to h
 \quad(1\le i\le d).
\]
The supplied set contains the first \(2d\) arrows and \(P_1\to h\).  Consequently
\[
 |T|=2d+1=N-1,qquad
 D\setminus T=\{P_i\to h:2\le i\le d\},qquad
 |D\setminus T|=d-1=k.
\tag{9}
\]
Every nonroot vertex has one incoming tree arrow, every vertex is reached from \(0\), and the order consisting of \(0\), then all \(P_i,Q_i\), and then \(h\) is topological.  Thus \(T\) is a rooted spanning arborescence, \(D\) is acyclic, and \(e^\star=P_1\to h\) is present.  By \(\mathrm{def:graph\mbox{-}class}\),
\[
 (G^\star_{k,N},T,e^\star)\in\mathcal G_{N,k}.
\tag{10}
\]

Choose positive rational numbers \(h_i\) and rational \(b_i\) with \(b_i^2>4h_i\), and put \(H_0=\operatorname{diag}(h_1,\ldots,h_d)\).  Choose a rational symmetric positive-definite matrix \(H\), sufficiently close to \(H_0\), with the same diagonal; a further generic restriction on its off-diagonal entries will be imposed below.  In the vertex order \((0,P_1,\ldots,P_d,Q_1,\ldots,Q_d,h)\), set
\[
 \Sigma^\star=
 \begin{pmatrix}
  1&0&0&1\\
  0&H&H&0\\
  0&H&C_0I_d&b\\
  1&0&b^{\mathsf T}&M
 \end{pmatrix},
 \qquad b=(b_1,\ldots,b_d)^{\mathsf T}.
\tag{11}
\]
Choose rational \(C_0\) so that \(C_0I_d-H\succ0\).  The Schur complement of \(H\) in the \((P,Q)\)-principal block is \(C_0I_d-H\), so that principal block is positive definite.  Adding the independent \(0\)-coordinate preserves positive definiteness of the \((0,P,Q)\)-block.  Finally choose rational \(M\) larger than the last Schur-complement threshold.  Then
\[
 \Sigma^\star\succ0.
\tag{12}
\]

Write
\[
 a_i=\lambda_{0P_i},\qquad c_i=\lambda_{0Q_i},\qquad
 z_i=\lambda_{P_i h},\qquad z=(z_1,\ldots,z_d)^{\mathsf T},
 \qquad x=-Hz.
\]
The missing pairs are \(P_i\leftrightarrow Q_i\), \(P_i\leftrightarrow h\), and \(Q_i\leftrightarrow h\).  Direct substitution of (11) into the defining residual formula gives
\[
 0=-a_i-(Hz)_i,qquad
 0=b_i-c_i-(Hz)_i,qquad
 0=h_i+a_ic_i.
\tag{13}
\]
Since \(H\) is invertible, (13) is equivalent to
\[
 a_i=x_i,qquad c_i=x_i+b_i,qquad
 x_i^2+b_ix_i+h_i=0\quad(1\le i\le d),
 \qquad z=-H^{-1}x.
\tag{14}
\]
Each discriminant \(b_i^2-4h_i\) is positive.  Thus (14) has exactly \(2^d\) real solutions.  Under the invertible change \(z\mapsto x=-Hz\), the residual Jacobian in \((a,c,z)\) is nonsingular precisely when
\[
 det(H)\prod_{i=1}^d(2x_i+b_i)\ne0.
\tag{15}
\]
Indeed, the three equations for a fixed \(i\), expressed in \((a_i,c_i,x_i)\), have determinant up to sign \(a_i+c_i=2x_i+b_i\).  At a solution,
\[
 (2x_i+b_i)^2=b_i^2-4h_i>0,
\]
and \(\det H>0\).  Hence all \(2^d\) points are reduced.  Setting
\[
 \Omega=(I_N-\Lambda)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^\star(I_N-\Lambda)
\tag{16}
\]
at any point, equations (13) make exactly the missing-pair entries vanish.  The displayed topological order makes \(I_N-\Lambda\) unit triangular and invertible, and (12) plus congruence in (16) gives \(\Omega\succ0\).  Thus all \(2^d\) solutions are real supported positive-definite source lifts.

We may choose \(H\) so that the original coefficient \(z_1=\lambda_{e^\star}\) separates the solutions.  At \(H=H_0\), branches with different \(x_1\) already have different \(z_1=-x_1/h_1\).  If two branch vectors \(x\ne x'\) have the same first coordinate, choose \(j>1\) with \(x_j\ne x'_j\) and put \(H(s)=H_0+s(E_{1j}+E_{j1})\).  Differentiating the inverse gives
\[
 \left.\frac{d}{ds}\{z_1(x)-z_1(x')\}\right|_{s=0}
 =\frac{x_j-x'_j}{h_1h_j}\ne0.
\tag{17}
\]
For each of the finitely many branch pairs, equality of their first coordinates after applying \(-H^{-1}\) is therefore a proper algebraic condition on the off-diagonal entries of \(H\).  A finite union of proper algebraic subsets cannot contain a Euclidean neighborhood of \(H_0\), and rational matrices are dense.  We choose rational \(H\) outside this union while retaining positive definiteness.  Then the \(2^d\) values of \(z_1\) are distinct.

There are \(3d\) directed coordinates and exactly \(3d\) missing residuals.  Since all other pairs are bidirected,
\[
 |D|+|B|+|V|
 =3d+\left(\binom N2-3d\right)+N
 =\frac{N(N+1)}2=:M_0.
\tag{18}
\]
Replace the independent covariance coordinates in (11) by \(\Sigma^\star+\xi\), where the \(M_0\) entries of \(\xi\) are algebraically independent.  At any reduced solution \(v_0=(a,c,z)\), seek a formal solution
\[
 v(\xi)=v_0+\sum_{r\ge1}v_r(\xi),
\]
with \(v_r\) homogeneous of degree \(r\).  The degree-\(r\) residual equation is
\[
 J(v_0)v_r=-R_r(\xi,v_1,\ldots,v_{r-1}).
\tag{19}
\]
The Jacobian is invertible by (15), so (19) determines a unique \(v_r\) recursively.  Hence every displayed point has a formal section over the full covariance formal neighborhood.

If \(f\in P_G\), substituting any such section gives \(f(\Sigma^\star+\xi)=0\) in \(\mathbb C[[\xi]]\).  Translation by \(\Sigma^\star\) is an injective automorphism of the covariance polynomial ring and the entries of \(\xi\) are algebraically independent, so \(f=0\).  Therefore
\[
 P_G=(0),\qquad K_G=\mathbb C(\sigma_{ij}:i\le j).
\tag{20}
\]
By (18), \(L\) and \(K_G\) have the same transcendence degree, so the finitely generated field extension \(L/K_G\) is finite.  Equivalently, the generic-fiber algebra \(A_K\) is a finitely generated integral algebraic \(K_G\)-algebra and hence the field \(L\).

Partition the variables into singleton blocks \(A_i=(a_i)\), singleton blocks \(C_i=(c_i)\), and one size-\(d\) block \(Z=(z_1,\ldots,z_d)\).  The residual block degrees are bounded respectively by \(A_i+C_i\), \(A_i+Z\), and \(C_i+Z\).  Thus \(\mathrm{lem:multihomogeneous\mbox{-}bezout\mbox{-}isolated\mbox{-}bound}\) gives
\[
 [L:K_G]\le
 \left[\left(\prod_{i=1}^dA_iC_i\right)Z^d\right]
 \prod_{i=1}^d(A_i+C_i)(A_i+Z)(C_i+Z)=2^d.
\tag{21}
\]
For each \(i\), exactly two selections contribute \(A_iC_iZ\), which proves the last equality.  This count applies to the original residual equations and counts multiplicity after base change to \(\overline{K_G}\).

Conversely, each formal section defines a homomorphism from the integral incidence ring into \(\mathbb C[[\xi]]\) restricting to the common injective covariance translation.  Its image has transcendence degree at least \(M_0\), equal by (18) to the dimension of the incidence domain; its prime kernel consequently has height zero and is zero.  Passing to fraction fields gives a \(K_G\)-embedding of \(L\) into \(\operatorname{Frac}\mathbb C[[\xi]]\).  The \(2^d\) embeddings send \(z_1\) to series with distinct constant terms.  Therefore the minimal polynomial of \(z_1\) over \(K_G\) has at least \(2^d\) roots, and
\[
 2^d\le[K_G(z_1):K_G]\le[L:K_G]\le2^d.
\tag{22}
\]
Thus \(d_{e^\star}(G^\star_{k,N})=2^{k+1}\), and \(e^\star\) separates all conjugate branches.  Characteristic zero makes its minimal polynomial separable.  Clearing its coefficient denominators and excluding their zeros and its nonzero discriminant leaves a nonempty Zariski-open covariance set on which these roots remain distinct; \(\mathrm{thm:incidence\mbox{-}localization}\) identifies them with the finite queried-coordinate projection.

For \(n>N\), append a fully bidirected child \(w\) of \(0\), place \(0\to w\) in \(T\), write \(x_w=\lambda_{0w}\), and let \(s_w\) be the new covariance row and diagonal.  No missing residual involves \(w\).  Conditional on the old source coordinates and \(x_w\), covariance congruence is an invertible triangular polynomial change between the new allowed disturbance coordinates and \(s_w\).  Hence, for the old and new fields,
\[
 L_1=L_0(x_w,s_w),\qquad K_1=K_0(s_w),
\tag{23}
\]
where \(x_w\) and the entries of \(s_w\) are algebraically independent over \(L_0\).  The minimal polynomial of \(z_1\) stays irreducible under the purely transcendental base extension \(K_0(s_w)/K_0\), so
\[
 [K_1(z_1):K_1]=[K_0(z_1):K_0]=2^d.
\tag{24}
\]
Iteration proves the degree assertion for every \(n\ge2k+4\).  Membership is preserved because each new arrow is a tree arrow and introduces no excess.  The upper bound \(D_k(n)\le2^{k+1}\) follows from \(\mathrm{thm:orientation\mbox{-}upper\mbox{-}bound}\), while (22)--(24) give the reverse inequality.  Therefore
\[
 D_k(n)=2^{k+1}\qquad(n\ge2k+4),
\]
 with the asserted nonempty Zariski-open separation set.

Condition on the successful symbolic event in \(\mathrm{thm:conditional\mbox{-}geometric\mbox{-}resolution}\).  By that theorem and its Schwartz--Zippel allocation, this event has probability at least \(1-\delta\).  Every circuit retained in \(\mathcal Q_{G,e}\) has nonzero pullback under the covariance parametrization.  Its class in the integral domain \(R_G\cong\operatorname{im}\phi_G\) is therefore nonzero.  The finite product of these classes is nonzero, so the cleared product \(h_{G,e}\) is not zero on the model image.  Hence
\[
 \mathcal E_{G,e}=V(h_{G,e})
\tag{32}
\]
is a proper algebraic subset of that image.

The relation \(p_e(\lambda_e)=0\) holds in the localized integral algebra \(A_K\).  Clearing only covariance denominators gives \(a\in S_G\) and incidence polynomials \(c_{ij}\) such that
\[
 a(\Sigma)p_e(\Sigma,\lambda_e)
 =\sum_{i\leftrightarrow j\notin B}
 c_{ij}(\Sigma,\Lambda)F_{ij}(\Lambda,\Sigma).
\tag{33}
\]
The factor \(a\) is included among the covariance-localization circuits.  Thus, whenever \(h_{G,e}(\Sigma)\ne0\), every solution of all specialized original residuals satisfies \(p_e(\Sigma,\lambda_e)=0\).  By the definition of \(\mathcal Z_e\),
\[
 \mathcal Z_e(G,\Sigma)
 \subseteq\{z\in\mathbb C:p_e(\Sigma,z)=0\}.
\tag{34}
\]

For the reverse inclusion, put \(E=K_G(\lambda_e)\).  For each \(K_G\)-embedding \(\tau:E\to\overline{K_G}\), the algebra \(L\otimes_{E,\tau}\overline{K_G}\) is nonzero.  The coordinate-preserving slices in the conditional algorithm were chosen from the common nonempty open set that meets every such conjugate component.  Their zero-dimensional rational univariate representations therefore contain every conjugate of \(\lambda_e\).  By \(\mathrm{lem:generic\mbox{-}rur\mbox{-}specialization}\), these representations specialize with finite points and multiplicities preserved away from the algebraic loci where dimension, a denominator, a leading coefficient, a point at infinity, or separation degenerates.  Every one of those loci contributes a factor to \(h_{G,e}\).  The returned incidence-lifting identities verify, by substitution, that each specialized univariate point satisfies every original residual.  Therefore every root of the specialized \(p_e\) lifts to the original incidence scheme, and
\[
 \{z\in\mathbb C:p_e(\Sigma,z)=0\}
 \subseteq\mathcal Z_e(G,\Sigma).
\tag{35}
\]
The slice is used only to produce the certificate; the lifting identities return to \(I_G\), so (35) does not require the unsliced \(\Lambda\)-fiber to be zero-dimensional.

Equations (34)--(35) prove the asserted equality.  Pole and incidence-lifting factors retain components on which an intermediate expression has a pole or is identically zero-over-zero.  Projective leading-form and specialized-leading-coefficient factors prevent exchange of a finite point with a point at infinity and prevent a degree drop.  Finally, characteristic zero makes \(p_e\) separable over \(K_G\); outside the squarefreeness resultant factor in \(h_{G,e}\), the specialization remains squarefree.  Hence its displayed roots are distinct.

Write \(s=(s_{ij}:i\le j)\) for real symmetric covariance variables, \(z\) for the queried value, and \(\ell=(\ell_f:f\in D)\) for real directed-coefficient variables.  Define the ordered-field formula
\[
 \Phi_G(s,z)\ \Longleftrightarrow\
 \exists\ell\in\mathbb R^D\left[
   \ell_e=z\ \wedge\
   \bigwedge_{i\leftrightarrow j\notin B}F_{ij}(\ell,s)=0
 \right].
\tag{36}
\]
Every polynomial in (36) has rational coefficients: \(D\) and \(B\) merely choose variables and equations, while each residual uses coefficients \(0,1,-1\).  By \(\mathrm{def:real\mbox{-}retained\mbox{-}set}\),
\[
 \Phi_G(\Sigma,z)
 \Longleftrightarrow z\in\mathcal R_e(G,\Sigma).
\tag{37}
\]

Apply \(\mathrm{lem:effective\mbox{-}real\mbox{-}quantifier\mbox{-}elimination}\) with \(\ell\) quantified and \((s,z)\) free.  It produces effectively a finite quantifier-free Boolean combination
\[
 \Psi_G(s,z)=\bigvee_a\bigwedge_b
 \bigl(\operatorname{sign}g_{ab}(s,z)=\epsilon_{ab}\bigr),
 \qquad g_{ab}\in\mathbb Q[s,z],\quad
 \epsilon_{ab}\in\{-1,0,1\},
\tag{38}
\]
equivalent to \(\Phi_G\) over every real closed field.  Equations (37)--(38) give the required computable if-and-only-if condition.  Because (36) uses the original residual equations and performs no division, it covers positive-dimensional fibers and components lying inside denominator-zero loci of intermediate reductions.

Now impose the valid-chart and successful-output antecedents.  For real \(\Sigma\succ0\) in the model image and outside \(\mathcal E_{G,e}\), \(\mathrm{thm:exceptional\mbox{-}set\mbox{-}validity}\) gives
\[
 \{z\in\mathbb C:p_e(\Sigma,z)=0\}
 =\mathcal Z_e(G,\Sigma).
\tag{39}
\]
The nonzero squarefreeness factor makes every root simple.  Formula (38) then determines, root by root, precisely whether the real root has a complete real supported extension.  In particular, no conclusion about real uniqueness is inferred from complex degree or a local Jacobian.

Suppose next that all entries of \(\Sigma\) have exact real-algebraic univariate representations and isolating data.  Every coefficient circuit of \(p_e\) can be evaluated exactly because all certified denominators are nonzero.  After clearing a known nonzero common denominator, \(\mathrm{lem:real\mbox{-}algebraic\mbox{-}sampling}\) applied to the resulting univariate equation returns a point on every connected component of its real zero set.  The polynomial is squarefree, so those components are its individual real roots.  Exact sign determination orders them and produces disjoint isolating intervals.

For such a root \(z\), exact sign determination evaluates (38).  Equivalently, define
\[
 Q_{\Sigma,z}(\ell)
 =(\ell_e-z)^2+
 \sum_{i\leftrightarrow j\notin B}F_{ij}(\ell,\Sigma)^2.
\tag{40}
\]
Over an ordered field, a sum of squares vanishes exactly when every summand vanishes.  Therefore
\[
 Z_{\mathbb R}(Q_{\Sigma,z})\ne\varnothing
 \Longleftrightarrow\Phi_G(\Sigma,z)
 \Longleftrightarrow z\in\mathcal R_e(G,\Sigma).
\tag{41}
\]
In the accepting case, real algebraic sampling applied to (40), over the ordered algebraic coefficient domain generated by \(\Sigma\) and \(z\), returns a real univariate representation of a complete lift \(\ell\).  In the rejecting case, the evaluated sign vector in (38) certifies failure.  A finite tower of algebraic coefficients can be encoded by one primitive real algebraic element: at each adjoining step only finitely many rational linear combinations fail to separate conjugate tuples, and an isolating interval selects the intended real embedding.  Thus the root representation, isolating interval, exact sign data, and, when accepting, the sample-point representation form a finite \(\mathsf{LiftCert}\), accepting exactly the elements of \(\mathcal R_e(G,\Sigma)\).

Finally let \(\Lambda\in\mathbb R^D\) be an accepted lift and put \(R=I_n-\Lambda\).  By \(\mathrm{ass:acyclic}\), a topological order makes \(\Lambda\) strictly triangular, so \(R\) is unit triangular and invertible.  Define
\[
 \Omega=R^{\mathsf T}\Sigma R.
\tag{42}
\]
For every nonzero real \(x\), invertibility gives \(Rx\ne0\), whence
\[
 x^{\mathsf T}\Omega x=(Rx)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(Rx)>0.
\]
Thus \(\Omega\succ0\).  Entrywise expansion of (42) is exactly
\[
 \Omega_{ij}=F_{ij}(\Lambda,\Sigma).
\tag{43}
\]
The accepting equations make (43) zero whenever \(i\leftrightarrow j\notin B\), which is precisely \(\mathrm{ass:noise\mbox{-}support}\).  Conversely, every real supported SEM lift satisfies those residual equations.  Equation (42) also rearranges to \(\Sigma=R^{-\mathsf T}\Omega R^{-1}\).  Hence the certificate retains all and only the real supported extensions, and positive definiteness follows by congruence as claimed.

Work under the valid-chart and successful-output antecedents.  On this event, \(\mathrm{thm:exceptional\mbox{-}set\mbox{-}validity}\) says that \(h_{G,e}\) is nonzero in the covariance-model coordinate ring.  Identify the free real entries of \((\Lambda,\Omega)\), subject only to the graph support, with \(\mathbb R^N\), where
\[
 N=|D|+|B|+n.
\]
The supported positive-definite source set
\[
 \mathcal S_+=\{(\Lambda,\Omega)\in\mathbb R^N:\Omega\succ0\}
\tag{44}
\]
is nonempty because it contains \((0,I_n)\), and is Euclidean open because strict positive definiteness is stable under small perturbations.  It is Zariski dense in the corresponding complex source space: it contains a real open box about \((0,I_n)\); a complex polynomial vanishing on that box is zero by successively regarding it as a univariate polynomial in each coordinate.

For the fixed acyclic graph, define
\[
 \Phi_G(\Lambda,\Omega)
 =(I_n-\Lambda)^{-\mathsf T}\Omega(I_n-\Lambda)^{-1}.
\tag{45}
\]
In a topological order \(\Lambda^n=0\), so each inverse is the finite polynomial \(I_n+\Lambda+\cdots+\Lambda^{n-1}\); hence \(\Phi_G\) is polynomial.  Nonzeroness of \(h_{G,e}\) in \(R_G\) means that \(h_{G,e}\circ\Phi_G\) is a nonzero source polynomial.  Zariski density of (44) supplies \((\Lambda_0,\Omega_0)\in\mathcal S_+\) with
\[
 h_{G,e}(\Phi_G(\Lambda_0,\Omega_0))\ne0.
\]
Putting \(\Sigma_0=\Phi_G(\Lambda_0,\Omega_0)\) gives
\[
 \Sigma_0\in\mathcal M_G\setminus\mathcal E_{G,e}.
\tag{46}
\]

The model image is semialgebraic: it is the projection of the source set defined by the polynomial covariance identities, the linear missing-support equalities, and the strict principal-minor inequalities for \(\Omega\succ0\); \(\mathrm{lem:effective\mbox{-}real\mbox{-}quantifier\mbox{-}elimination}\) removes the source variables.  The exceptional complement and every real-lifting sign condition are semialgebraic.  Outside the leading-coefficient and squarefreeness factors, the degree of \(p_e(\Sigma,\cdot)\) is fixed and all roots are simple.  The assertion that \(z\) is the \(j\)-th ordered real root is a first-order ordered-field formula, and quantifier elimination makes its graph semialgebraic.  Intersecting that graph with the lifting formula and projecting shows that the locus on which the \(j\)-th root is extendable is semialgebraic.

Apply \(\mathrm{lem:semialgebraic\mbox{-}stratification}\) to the finite common refinement by the model image, the exceptional complement, the possible real-root counts, and all extendability loci, and then take connected components.  The component through \(\Sigma_0\) is a connected smooth semialgebraic cell
\[
 \mathcal C_{G,e}\subseteq
 \mathcal M_G\setminus\mathcal E_{G,e}
\tag{47}
\]
on which the number of simple real roots and every ordered root's extension label are constant.  This is the cell in \(\mathrm{def:regular\mbox{-}cell}\).

Choose a smooth coordinate chart \(u:U\to u(U)\subseteq\mathbb R^s\) about \(\Sigma_0\).  If \(s>0\), choose \(\rho>0\) with \(\overline B(u(\Sigma_0),\rho)\subset u(U)\), and set
\[
 \mathcal K_G=u^{-1}\!\left(\overline B(u(\Sigma_0),\rho)\right).
\tag{48}
\]
If \(s=0\), set \(\mathcal K_G=\{\Sigma_0\}\).  In both cases \(\mathcal K_G\) is nonempty, compact, and has nonempty relative interior in \(\mathcal C_{G,e}\), as required by \(\mathrm{def:regular\mbox{-}class}\).

For any \(\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G\), membership in \(\mathcal M_G\) supplies real supported \(\Lambda\) and \(\Omega\succ0\) satisfying (45).  Rearrangement gives
\[
 \Omega=(I_n-\Lambda)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(I_n-\Lambda).
\]
At every missing bidirected pair, its entry is \(F_{ij}(\Lambda,\Sigma)=0\).  Hence the real value \(\lambda_e\) has a complete real supported extension and belongs to \(\mathcal R_e(G,\Sigma)\).  Thus \(\mathcal R_e(G,\Sigma)\ne\varnothing\) everywhere on \(\mathcal K_G\).

Put \(d=d_e(G)\).  On the successful output the finite monic polynomial specializes as
\[
 p_e(\Sigma,t)=t^d+\sum_{a=0}^{d-1}c_a(\Sigma)t^a.
\tag{49}
\]
Each \(c_a\) is a rational covariance circuit.  Since \(\mathcal K_G\subset\mathcal M_G\setminus\mathcal E_{G,e}\), every denominator, specialized-leading-coefficient, and squarefreeness certificate factor is continuous and nonzero on \(\mathcal K_G\).  Compactness gives a positive minimum for the absolute value of each denominator and a finite maximum for every numerator.  Therefore some \(M<\infty\) satisfies
\[
 \max_{0\le a<d}|c_a(\Sigma)|\le M
 \quad(\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G).
\tag{50}
\]
If \(z\) is a root and \(|z|>1+M\), then
\[
 |z|^d
 \le M\sum_{a=0}^{d-1}|z|^a
 =M\frac{|z|^d-1}{|z|-1}
 <|z|^d,
\]
a contradiction.  Thus every root lies in the fixed disk \(|z|\le1+M\).  The incidence set
\[
 \mathcal Z_{\mathrm{root}}=\{(\Sigma,z)\in\mathcal K_G\times\mathbb C:
 p_e(\Sigma,z)=0\}
\tag{51}
\]
is closed in a compact set and hence compact.

The nonzero squarefreeness certificate says that \(p_e(\Sigma,\cdot)\) and \(\partial_tp_e(\Sigma,\cdot)\) have no common root.  Consequently \(\partial_tp_e\ne0\) on (51), and continuity gives
\[
 \eta=\min_{(\Sigma,z)\in\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{root}}}
 |\partial_tp_e(\Sigma,z)|>0.
\tag{52}
\]
If no uniform root separation existed, there would be \(\Sigma_\nu\in\mathcal K_G\) and distinct roots \(z_\nu,w_\nu\) with \(|z_\nu-w_\nu|\to0\).  Compactness yields a subsequence with
\[
 \Sigma_\nu\to\Sigma_*,\qquad z_\nu\to z_*,\qquad w_\nu\to z_*.
\]
The divided difference
\[
 \frac{p_e(\Sigma,z)-p_e(\Sigma,w)}{z-w}
\]
extends polynomially to the diagonal with value \(\partial_tp_e(\Sigma,z)\).  It vanishes at \((\Sigma_\nu,z_\nu,w_\nu)\), so the limit satisfies both \(p_e(\Sigma_*,z_*)=0\) and \(\partial_tp_e(\Sigma_*,z_*)=0\), contradicting (52).  Hence a \(\gamma>0\) uniformly separates all distinct complex roots.  By exceptional-set validity and real-root lifting, every retained real value is one of these roots, so the same \(\gamma\) separates the retained roots.

Let \(q=n(n+1)/2\), fix an ordering \(\operatorname{vech}\) of symmetric entries, and set
\[
 W_r=\operatorname{vech}\!\left(
 X^{(r)}X^{(r)\mathsf T}-\Sigma\right).
\]
Then
\[
 \sqrt m\,\operatorname{vech}(S_m-\Sigma)
 =m^{-1/2}\sum_{r=1}^mW_r.
\tag{53}
\]
By \(\mathrm{ass:iid\mbox{-}gaussian}\), the summands are independent and centered.  Differentiating the Gaussian moment-generating function gives
\[
 \mathbb E(X_iX_jX_kX_l)
 =\sigma_{ij}\sigma_{kl}+\sigma_{ik}\sigma_{jl}
  +\sigma_{il}\sigma_{jk},
\]
and consequently
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}(W_{r,ij},W_{r,kl})
 =\sigma_{ik}\sigma_{jl}+\sigma_{il}\sigma_{jk}
 =(V_\Sigma)_{ij,kl}.
\tag{54}
\]

Compactness of \(\mathcal K_G\) uniformly bounds all fixed Gaussian moments, including \(\mathbb E_\Sigma\|W_r\|^3\).  Taylor expansion of \(e^{ix}\) therefore gives, for fixed \(u\in\mathbb R^q\), uniformly in \(\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G\),
\[
 \mathbb E_\Sigma\exp\!\left(
 \frac{iu^{\mathsf T}W_r}{\sqrt m}\right)
 =1-\frac{u^{\mathsf T}V_\Sigma u}{2m}+O(m^{-3/2}).
\tag{55}
\]
Taking the \(m\)-th power proves the covariance central limit law.  Uniformity follows by the subsequence principle: every sequence \(\Sigma_m\in\mathcal K_G\) has a convergent subsequence, (55) identifies every weak subsequential limit, and the uniformly bounded second moments give tightness.  Hence
\[
 \sqrt m\,\operatorname{vech}(S_m-\Sigma)
 \rightsquigarrow N(0,V_\Sigma)
\tag{56}
\]
uniformly on \(\mathcal K_G\), and Chebyshev's inequality gives
\[
 \|S_m-\Sigma\|=O_{\mathbb P}(m^{-1/2})
\tag{57}
\]
uniformly.

Write \(\widehat\Sigma_m=\pi_G(S_m)\) on the projection tube.  Because \(\pi_G(\Sigma)=\Sigma\) on the smooth stratum, smoothness and compactness give the uniform Taylor expansion
\[
 \operatorname{vech}(\widehat\Sigma_m-\Sigma)
 =D\pi_G(\Sigma)\operatorname{vech}(S_m-\Sigma)
  +O_{\mathbb P}(\|S_m-\Sigma\|^2).
\tag{58}
\]
Every coefficient circuit of \(p_e\) is smooth near \(\mathcal K_G\), since its denominators are bounded away from zero.  The derived separation lemma supplies a common separation margin and a positive lower bound for \(|\partial_tp_e|\) at every root.  The implicit-function calculation therefore produces one unique smooth branch through every retained root, with uniformly bounded first and second derivatives on a finite cover of \(\mathcal K_G\), and
\[
 Dr_j(\Sigma)[H]
 =-\frac{D_\Sigma p_e(\Sigma,r_j(\Sigma))[H]}
         {\partial_tp_e(\Sigma,r_j(\Sigma))}.
\tag{59}
\]
Increasing order, separation, and constancy of the extension labels on the connected regular cell give the common labeling \(r=(r_1,\ldots,r_J)\).  Combining (56)--(59) gives, uniformly on \(\mathcal K_G\),
\[
 \sqrt m\{r(\pi_G(S_m))-r(\Sigma)\}
 \rightsquigarrow N\!\left(0,
 Dr(\Sigma)D\pi_G(\Sigma)V_\Sigma
 D\pi_G(\Sigma)^{\mathsf T}Dr(\Sigma)^{\mathsf T}
 \right).
\tag{60}
\]

Every certificate factor is continuous and nonzero on \(\mathcal K_G\), and all extension labels are locally constant on the selected cell.  Compactness therefore supplies a relative neighborhood \(U\) on which the projection is defined, every certificate stays valid, and the same \(J\) branches are retained.  Let \(\gamma\) be the derived separation margin and define
\[
 \mathcal H_m=\left\{
 \begin{array}{l}
 S_m\text{ lies in the projection tube},\quad
 \widehat\Sigma_m\in U,\\[2pt]
 \displaystyle\max_{1\le j\le J}
 |r_j(\widehat\Sigma_m)-r_j(\Sigma)|<\gamma/3
 \end{array}\right\}.
\tag{61}
\]
Uniform consistency in (57)--(58), uniform continuity of the roots, and the positive certificate margins imply
\[
 \inf_{\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G}\Pr_\Sigma(\mathcal H_m)\to1.
\tag{62}
\]
On \(\mathcal H_m\), the real-lifting theorem and \(\mathrm{def:finite\mbox{-}set\mbox{-}estimator}\) give
\[
 \widehat{\mathcal R}_{e,m}
 =\{r_1(\widehat\Sigma_m),\ldots,r_J(\widehat\Sigma_m)\}.
\tag{63}
\]
The separation in (61) makes (63) a bijective matching to \(\mathcal R_e(G,\Sigma)\).  The regular-cell lemma gives \(J\ge1\), so it is nonempty.  Moreover,
\[
 d_H\!\left(\widehat{\mathcal R}_{e,m},
             \mathcal R_e(G,\Sigma)\right)
 \le\max_j|r_j(\widehat\Sigma_m)-r_j(\Sigma)|
 =O_{\mathbb P}(m^{-1/2})
\tag{64}
\]
uniformly.  Although the stipulated Hausdorff distance can be infinite on \(\mathcal H_m^c\), (62) makes that event uniformly negligible, which is exactly the definition of the uniform \(O_{\mathbb P}\) claim.  Also
\[
 \sup_{\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G}
 \Pr_\Sigma(\widehat{\mathcal R}_{e,m}=\varnothing)
 \le\sup_{\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G}\Pr_\Sigma(\mathcal H_m^c)
 \to0.
\tag{65}
\]

For simultaneous neighborhoods, let \(s=\dim\mathcal C_{G,e}\) and
\[
 W_\pi(\Sigma)=D\pi_G(\Sigma)V_\Sigma D\pi_G(\Sigma)^{\mathsf T}.
\]
For a nonzero symmetric direction \(H\), the Gaussian fourth-moment identity gives
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_\Sigma(X^{\mathsf T}HX)
 =2\operatorname{tr}\!\left((\Sigma^{1/2}H\Sigma^{1/2})^2\right)>0.
\tag{66}
\]
Thus \(V_\Sigma\) is positive definite on symmetric-coordinate directions.  Since the nearest-point projection fixes the stratum, \(D\pi_G\) is the identity on its tangent space and has that \(s\)-dimensional space as image.  Hence \(W_\pi\) has constant rank \(s\); compactness bounds its smallest positive eigenvalue away from zero, so its Moore--Penrose inverse is continuous.  With the plug-in matrix \(\widehat W_{\pi,m}\), equations (56)--(58) and continuous mapping give
\[
 m\,\operatorname{vech}(\widehat\Sigma_m-\Sigma)^{\mathsf T}
 \widehat W_{\pi,m}^{+}
 \operatorname{vech}(\widehat\Sigma_m-\Sigma)
 \rightsquigarrow\chi_s^2
\tag{67}
\]
uniformly.  Indeed, if \(Z\sim N(0,W_\pi)\), then \(Z^{\mathsf T}W_\pi^+Z\) is a sum of \(s\) independent squared standard normals.

Let \(E_m\) be the corresponding confidence ellipsoid centered at \(\widehat\Sigma_m\), intersected with the regular projected neighborhood, using the \((1-\alpha)\)-quantile of \(\chi_s^2\).  Equation (67) yields
\[
 \liminf_{m\to\infty}\inf_{\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G}
 \Pr_\Sigma(\Sigma\in E_m)\ge1-\alpha.
\tag{68}
\]
For \(s=0\), use the degenerate ellipsoid at the locally constant projected point, with limiting coverage one.  As in \(\mathrm{def:branch\mbox{-}neighborhoods}\), set \(\mathcal A_{m,j}=r_j(E_m)\).  Whenever \(\Sigma\in E_m\), all inclusions \(r_j(\Sigma)\in\mathcal A_{m,j}\) hold simultaneously.  Therefore
\[
 \liminf_{m\to\infty}\inf_{\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G}
 \Pr_\Sigma\!\left(
 r_j(\Sigma)\in\mathcal A_{m,j}\text{ for all }1\le j\le J
 \right)\ge1-\alpha.
\]
This covers every retained branch and selects none.

Assume \(\mathcal R_e(G,\Sigma)=\{r_1(\Sigma)\}\) throughout \(\mathcal K_G\).  On the events \(\mathcal H_m\) from \(\mathrm{thm:regular\mbox{-}finite\mbox{-}set\mbox{-}inference}\), the estimated set is bijectively matched to this singleton.  Hence it has exactly one element, denoted \(\widehat r_m\), and
\[
 \inf_{\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G}\Pr_\Sigma\!\left(
 \widehat{\mathcal R}_{e,m}=\{\widehat r_m\}\right)\to1.
\tag{69}
\]
Define \(\widehat r_m=0\) outside that event; (69) makes this modification uniformly negligible.  For singleton sets the Hausdorff distance is absolute error, so the rate conclusion of the cited theorem gives
\[
 |\widehat r_m-r_1(\Sigma)|
 =O_{\mathbb P}(m^{-1/2})
\]
uniformly, proving consistency.  Taking the first coordinate of its joint branch limit gives
\[
 \sqrt m\{\widehat r_m-r_1(\Sigma)\}
 \rightsquigarrow N(0,W_{11}(\Sigma)),
\]
where
\[
 W(\Sigma)=Dr(\Sigma)D\pi_G(\Sigma)V_\Sigma
 D\pi_G(\Sigma)^{\mathsf T}Dr(\Sigma)^{\mathsf T}.
\]
The negligible modification does not affect this limit.  If \(W_{11}(\Sigma)=0\), the notation denotes the degenerate centered normal law, so no unstated variance lower bound is needed.

Fix a source-consistent recorded stratum and use \(\mathrm{def:source\mbox{-}prime\mbox{-}chart}\).  Thus \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_r)\), \(r\le2k\), \(P=\ker\xi\subset K_G[x]\), and validity of the supplied chart gives
\[
 P K_G[x]_{H\Delta}
 =(h_1,\ldots,h_c)K_G[x]_{H\Delta},
 \qquad \xi(H\Delta)\ne0,
\tag{25}
\]
where \(c=\operatorname{ht}P\), the localized sequence is reduced and regular, and \(\Delta\) is a nonzero \(c\)-by-\(c\) Jacobian minor.  Thus (25) presents the localization of the source prime, not an extraneous residual component.  It is smooth and pure-dimensional of dimension
\[
 q=r-c\le2k.
\tag{26}
\]
The principal open set \(H\Delta\ne0\) may be encoded by adjoining \(u\) and the equation \(uH\Delta-1=0\).

Put \(E=K_G(\lambda_e)\).  Since \(d_e(G)<\infty\), \(E/K_G\) is finite and separable.  For every \(K_G\)-embedding \(\tau:E\to\overline{K_G}\), the algebra
\[
 L\otimes_{E,\tau}\overline{K_G}
\]
is nonzero: after choosing an \(E\)-transcendence basis of \(L\), the remaining extension is algebraic, and tensoring a nonzero field extension with the faithfully flat field \(\overline{K_G}\) cannot annihilate it.  Hence the base change of the source-prime chart has a nonempty component for every conjugate of \(\lambda_e\), and \(H\Delta\) is nonzero on each component.

Generic affine hyperplanes meet every positive-dimensional component properly.  There are only \(d_e(G)\) conjugate components, so the intersection of their nonempty open sets of admissible hyperplane choices is nonempty.  Choose \(q\) affine linear forms whose successive intersections are transverse, zero-dimensional, and nonempty on every conjugate component.  This is precisely the transverse slicing operation in \(\mathrm{lem:groebner\mbox{-}free\mbox{-}geometric\mbox{-}resolution}\).  Random choices outside the finitely many determinant and leading-form hypersurfaces satisfy it.

Apply that geometric-resolution result to the localized regular sequence and these \(q\) slices.  On successful choices it returns a finite reduced algebra \(B_{\mathfrak C}\), multiplication matrices for the exposed coordinates, and a primitive-element representation.  The chart's rational lifting circuits recover every eliminated directed coordinate, including \(\lambda_e\), and their defining validity identities make every original residual vanish in the localized source-prime algebra.  Let \(M_{e,\mathfrak C}\) be multiplication by the recovered \(\lambda_e\) on \(B_{\mathfrak C}\), and define
\[
 \chi_{e,\mathfrak C}(t)=\det(tI-M_{e,\mathfrak C}).
\tag{27}
\]
Every point encoded by (27) lies on a base change of the source prime, so its queried coordinate is a conjugate of \(\lambda_e\).  Conversely, the common slices meet every conjugate component, so every conjugate occurs in at least one chart.  Therefore
\[
 p_e(t)=\operatorname{sqfree}\!\left(
   \prod_{\mathfrak C}\chi_{e,\mathfrak C}(t)
 \right),
 \qquad \deg p_e=d_e(G).
\tag{28}
\]
The equality follows from uniqueness of the monic polynomial whose roots are exactly the distinct conjugates.  It concerns the single coordinate even if the unsliced fiber is positive-dimensional.  The degree is finite and is bounded by \(\mathrm{thm:orientation\mbox{-}upper\mbox{-}bound}\).

All chart coefficients and lifting maps are rational arithmetic circuits in the covariance entries.  Determinants, multiplication-matrix operations, differentiation, subresultant greatest-common-divisor computation, squarefree extraction, and monic normalization are arithmetic-circuit operations over \(K_G\), so (28) supplies coefficientwise rational circuits for \(p_e\).  For each lifting identity, clearing covariance denominators records both its denominator and the resulting original-incidence identity.  Homogenization before slicing records projective leading forms; univariate normalization records the specialized leading coefficient and squarefreeness resultant.  The covariance-localization factors are kept separately.  Real sign-determination data are computed on the at-most-\(2k\)-coordinate chart and checked after substitution in the original residuals.  These finitely many nonzero circuits form \(\mathcal Q_{G,e}\), and their repetition-free cleared product is \(h_{G,e}\).  Equality (25) and \(\mathrm{thm:incidence\mbox{-}localization}\) ensure that no directed-coordinate expression is inverted, so pole and identically zero-over-zero strata are either represented by their own supplied valid chart or retained in the original incidence checks.

For arbitrary recorded equations and inequations, use \(\mathrm{lem:lifting\mbox{-}fiber\mbox{-}equidimensional\mbox{-}decomposition}\); for the regular localized slices use \(\mathrm{lem:groebner\mbox{-}free\mbox{-}geometric\mbox{-}resolution}\).  Their stated arithmetic bounds, the chart dimension (26), multiplication-matrix linear algebra, and exact sign determination on the returned univariate and lifting representations give a universal \(a>0\) for which the total arithmetic work and the number of output gates are bounded by
\[
 (n+s)^{a(k+1)}\mathfrak d^a
 \operatorname{poly}(\log(1/\delta)),
\tag{29}
\]
where \(s=s(\mathfrak C_{G,e})\) and \(\mathfrak d=\mathfrak d(\mathfrak C_{G,e})\).  Here \(\mathfrak d\) includes the successive chart intersections, localizations, slices, and lifting fibers, exactly as specified in the chart definition, so (29) charges every branch created by these operations.

Every randomized decision is a nonvanishing test for an explicitly constructed chart, transversality, leading-form, lifting, or resultant polynomial.  If their degree bounds are \(d_1,\ldots,d_N\), sample independently from finite sets \(S_j\) with \(d_j/|S_j|\le\delta/N\).  By \(\mathrm{lem:schwartz\mbox{-}zippel\mbox{-}bound}\) and the union bound,
\[
 \Pr(\text{some symbolic genericity decision is wrong})
 \le\sum_{j=1}^N\frac{d_j}{|S_j|}\le\delta.
\tag{30}
\]
On the complementary event, (25)--(28) prove that the returned tuple is exactly \((d_e(G),p_e,\mathcal Q_{G,e},h_{G,e})\).

If \(s\le n^b\) and \(\mathfrak d\le n^{b(k+1)}\), then, enlarging a universal constant for \(n\ge2\),
\[
 (n+s)^{a(k+1)}\mathfrak d^a
 \le n^{a(\max\{1,b\}+1+b)(k+1)}
 \le n^{C(k+1)}.
\tag{31}
\]
This proves the stated fixed-parameter specialization.  The conclusion is conditional exactly as stated: the cited equation-solving algorithms act after a valid localized source-prime chart is supplied; they do not select that embedded prime component or construct the required source-nonzero Jacobian minor.

For a finite simple graph \(H=(W,E_H)\) and \(r=(r_v:v\in W)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^W\), put
\[
 c_H(r)=\left[\prod_{v\in W}X_v^{r_v}\right]
 \prod_{\{u,v\}\in E_H}(X_u+X_v).
\tag{70}
\]
Choosing \(X_v\) from the factor for \(\{u,v\}\) is the same as orienting that edge toward \(v\).  Hence \(c_H(r)\) counts orientations with indegree vector \(r\), and
\[
 c_H(r)=0\quad\text{unless}\quad
 \sum_{v\in W}r_v=|E_H|,
 \qquad 0\le r_v\le\deg_H(v).
\tag{71}
\]

On at most two vertices, simplicity leaves at most one edge and its direction is fixed by \(r\), so the count is at most one.  On at most three vertices, a forest also has at most one orientation with prescribed indegrees: the direction at a leaf is forced and induction deletes the leaf.  For the triangle, the two directed cycles both have vector \((1,1,1)\), whereas each transitive tournament is uniquely determined by its labeled score permutation \((0,1,2)\).  Thus the maximum on three vertices is two.

Now let \(|W|\le4\).  With at most four edges, each connected component is a tree except possibly one unicyclic component.  Leaf deletion forces every edge outside the unique cycle, and at most its two cyclic orientations remain.  Thus
\[
 c_H(r)\le2\qquad(|W|\le4,\ |E_H|\le4).
\tag{72}
\]
With five edges, \(H\) is \(K_4\) minus one edge, say \(\{1,2\}\).  For
\[
 P=(X_1+X_3)(X_1+X_4)(X_2+X_3)(X_2+X_4)(X_3+X_4),
\]
collecting terms according to the number \(a\) of \(X_1\)-choices in the first two factors and the number \(b\) of \(X_2\)-choices in the next two gives the exact coefficient-maxima table
\[
 \begin{array}{c|ccc}
  &b=0&b=1&b=2\\ \hline
 a=0&1&2&1\\
 a=1&2&3&2\\
 a=2&1&2&1.
 \end{array}
\tag{73}
\]
Indeed, before multiplying by \(X_3+X_4\), the four independent binomial choices have multiplicities \(\binom2a\binom2b\); the last choice shifts exactly one of the two remaining exponents, yielding (73) by direct collection.  Hence every five-edge coefficient is at most three.

With six edges, \(H=K_4\).  Up to sorting, the vectors satisfying (71) are
\[
 (0,0,3,3),\ (0,1,2,3),\ (0,2,2,2),\
 (1,1,1,3),\ (1,1,2,2).
\tag{74}
\]
The first has coefficient zero because the edge between the two zero-score vertices has no allowed endpoint.  Type \((0,1,2,3)\) forces the unique transitive orientation.  In types \((0,2,2,2)\) and \((1,1,1,3)\), the extreme vertex's edges are forced and the remaining triangle has two cyclic orientations.  For \((1,1,2,2)\), condition on the edge \(12\).  If it points toward \(1\), the remaining edges incident with \(1\) point away, and the triangle on \(2,3,4\) has two compatible cyclic choices; the case in which edge \(12\) points toward \(2\) is symmetric.  Therefore
\[
 [X_1X_2X_3^2X_4^2]
 \prod_{1\le i<j\le4}(X_i+X_j)=2+2=4,
\tag{75}
\]
and four is the maximum on four blocks.

In the square subsystem selected in \(\mathrm{thm:orientation\mbox{-}upper\mbox{-}bound}\), variables are partitioned by child vertex.  The root of \(T\) has no incoming arrow: an arrow into it, combined with its tree path to the arrow's tail, would create a directed cycle.  Hence at most \(n-1\) blocks are nonempty.  The residual \(F_{ij}\) has degree at most one in each of the two child blocks \(i,j\), and an unordered pair supplies only one residual, so the binary-factor graph is simple.  By \(\mathrm{lem:multihomogeneous\mbox{-}bezout\mbox{-}isolated\mbox{-}bound}\), the relevant coefficient is (70).  The preceding counts give
\[
 d_e(G)\le1\quad(n=3),\qquad
 d_e(G)\le2\quad(n=4),\qquad
 d_e(G)\le4\quad(n=5).
\tag{76}
\]

If \(n=5\) and \(|D\setminus T|\le1\), then \(|D|\le5\), so the selected square system has at most five equations and, after removing unary factors, at most five binary factors.  Four or fewer give at most two by (72).  Five force four nonempty blocks, the graph \(K_4\setminus e\), no unary factor, and positive block sizes summing to five; their exponent vector is a permutation of \((2,1,1,1)\).  Table (73) bounds the coefficient by three.  Hence
\[
 d_e(G)\le3\qquad(n=5,\ |D\setminus T|\le1),
\]
which proves every assertion.

Write
\[
 (a,b,c,d,u,f)=(\lambda_{01},\lambda_{02},\lambda_{13},
 \lambda_{23},\lambda_{14},\lambda_{24}).
\]
The displayed \(T\) has four arrows, gives every nonroot exactly one parent, and reaches every vertex from \(0\); hence it is a rooted spanning arborescence.  Moreover
\[
 D\setminus T=\{2\to3,2\to4\},
\]
the order \(0<1<2<3<4\) is topological, and \(e=2\to4\).  Therefore \((G^{(4)},T,e)\in\mathcal G_{5,2}\) by \(\mathrm{def:graph\mbox{-}class}\).

At the rational source point
\[
 (a,b,c,d,u,f)=(2,3,4,5,6,7),
 \qquad
 \Omega^\star=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 30&1&2&3&4\\
 1&31&0&0&0\\
 2&0&32&0&0\\
 3&0&0&33&0\\
 4&0&0&0&34
 \end{pmatrix},
\tag{77}
\]
all nonzero off-diagonal disturbance entries are allowed by \(B\).  The inequality \(2|y_iy_j|\le y_i^2+y_j^2\) gives, for \(y\ne0\),
\[
 y^{\mathsf T}\Omega^\star y
 \ge20y_0^2+30y_1^2+30y_2^2+30y_3^2+30y_4^2>0,
\]
so \(\Omega^\star\succ0\).  Direct multiplication gives
\[
 \Sigma^\star=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 30&61&92&707&1014\\
 61&155&187&1561&2247\\
 92&187&314&2327&3332\\
 707&1561&2327&17981&25747\\
 1014&2247&3332&25747&36972
 \end{pmatrix}.
\tag{78}
\]
It is positive definite by congruence because \(I_5-\Lambda^\star\) is unit triangular.

The missing bidirected pairs are the six pairs inside \(\{1,2,3,4\}\).  Substitution into their residuals gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
